{{Short description|Statistical ensemble}}
{{Orphan|date=October 2025}}

The '''Gibbs rotational ensemble''' represents the possible states of a mechanical system in [[thermal equilibrium|thermal]] and rotational equilibrium at [[temperature]] <math>T</math> and [[angular velocity]] <math>\boldsymbol\omega</math>.<ref name="gibbs">{{cite book |last1=Gibbs |first1=Josiah Willard |title=Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics |date=2010 |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511686948 |isbn=978-1-108-01702-2 |authorlink1=Josiah Willard Gibbs }}{{page needed|date=August 2025}}</ref> The Jaynes procedure can be used to obtain this ensemble.<ref name=TD>{{cite report |type=Preprint |last1=Thomson |first1=Mitchell |last2=Dyer |first2=Charles C. |title=Black Hole Statistical Mechanics and the Angular Velocity Ensemble |date=2012 |arxiv=1203.6542 }}</ref> An [[Statistical Ensemble|ensemble]] is the set of [[microstate (statistical mechanics)|microstates]] corresponding to a given [[macrostate]].

The Gibbs rotational ensemble assigns a [[probability]] <math>p_i</math> to a given microstate characterized by [[energy]] <math>E_i</math> and [[angular momentum]] <math>\mathbf J_i</math> for a given temperature <math>T</math> and rotational velocity <math>\boldsymbol \omega</math>.<ref name="gibbs"/><ref name="gyro">{{cite journal |last1=Heims |first1=S. P. |last2=Jaynes |first2=E. T. |title=Theory of Gyromagnetic Effects and Some Related Magnetic Phenomena |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |date=April 1962 |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=143–165 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.34.143 |bibcode=1962RvMP...34..143H }}</ref>

<math display="block"> p_i = \frac{1}{Z} e^{-\beta (E_i - \boldsymbol\omega \cdot \mathbf J_i)} </math>

where <math>Z</math> is the [[partition function (statistical mechanics)|partition function]]

<math display="block"> Z = \sum_i e^{-\beta(E_i-\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf J_i)} </math>

==Derivation==
The Gibbs rotational ensemble can be derived using the same general method as to derive any ensemble, as given by [[E.T. Jaynes]] in his 1956 paper Information Theory and Statistical Mechanics.<ref name="gyro"/> Let <math>f(x)</math> be a [[function (math)|function]] with [[expectation value]]

<math display="block"> \langle f(x)\rangle = \sum_i p_i f(x_i) </math>

where <math>p_i</math> is the probability of <math>x_i</math>, which is not known [[a priori]]. The probabilities <math>p_i</math> obey [[normalization (statistics)|normalization]]

<math display="block"> \sum_i p_i = 1 </math>

To find <math>p_i</math>, the [[Claude Shannon|Shannon]] [[entropy]] <math>H</math> is [[maximize]]d, where the Shannon entropy goes as

<math display="block"> H \sim \sum_i p_i \ln(p_i) </math>

The method of [[Lagrange multipliers]] is used to maximize <math>H</math> under the constraints <math>\langle f(x)\rangle</math> and the normalization condition, using Lagrange multipliers <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\mu</math> to find

<math display="block"> p_i = e^{-\lambda-\mu f(x_i)} </math>

<math>\lambda</math> is found via normalization:

<math display="block"> \lambda = \ln\left(\sum_i e^{-\mu f(x_i)}\right) = \ln(Z(\mu)) </math>

and <math>\langle f(x)\rangle</math> can be written as

<math display="block">
 \langle f(x)\rangle = -\frac{\partial}{\partial \mu} \ln\left(\sum_i e^{-\mu f(x_i)}\right)=-\frac{\partial}{\partial \mu}\ln(Z(\mu))
</math>

where <math>Z</math> is the partition function

<math display="block">
 Z(\mu) = \sum_i e^{-\mu f(x_i)}
</math>

This is easily generalized to any number of equations <math>f(x)</math> via the incorporation of more Lagrange multipliers.<ref name="gyro"/>

Now investigating the Gibbs rotational ensemble, the method of Lagrange multipliers is again used to maximize the Shannon entropy <math>H</math>, but this time under the constraints of energy expectation value <math>\langle E\rangle</math> and angular momentum expectation value <math>\langle J\rangle</math>,<ref name="gyro"/> which gives <math>p_i</math> as

<math display="block"> p_i = e^{-\lambda_0 E_i - \boldsymbol \lambda_1 \cdot \mathbf J_i - \lambda_3} </math>

Via normalization, <math>\lambda_3</math> is found to be

<math display="block"> \lambda_3 = \ln\left(\sum_i e^{-\lambda_0 E_i-\boldsymbol \lambda_1 \cdot\mathbf J_i}\right) = \ln(Z) </math>

Like before, <math>\langle E\rangle</math> and <math>\langle J\rangle</math> are given by

<math display="block"> \langle E\rangle = -\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_0}\ln\left(\sum_i e^{-\lambda_0 E_i-\boldsymbol \lambda_1\cdot\mathbf J_i}\right)
= -\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_0} \ln\left(Z\right)</math>

<math display="block"> \langle J\rangle = -\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_1}\ln\left(\sum_i e^{-\lambda_0 E_i-\boldsymbol\lambda_1\cdot\mathbf J_i}\right)
= -\frac{\partial}{\partial\lambda_1} \ln(Z)</math>

The entropy <math>S</math> of the system is given by

<math display="block">S = -k\sum_i p_i\ln(p_i)=k(\lambda_0 \langle E\rangle +\boldsymbol\lambda_1\cdot\langle \mathbf{J} \rangle+\ln(Z))</math>

such that

<math display="block"> dS = k \left(\lambda_0 \mathrm{d}\langle E\rangle + \boldsymbol\lambda_1\mathrm{d}\langle \mathbf{J}\rangle + \mathrm{d}\ln(Z)\right)</math>

where <math>k</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]]. The [[thermodynamic system|system]] is assumed to be in equilibrium, follow the laws of [[thermodynamics]], and have fixed uniform temperature <math>T</math> and angular velocity <math>\boldsymbol\omega</math>. The [[first law of thermodynamics]] as applied to this system is

<math display="block"> \mathrm{d}E = \mathrm{d}Q+\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathrm{d}\langle \mathbf J\rangle</math>

Recalling the entropy differential
<math display="block"> \mathrm{d}S = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{T} </math>

Combining the first law of thermodynamics with the entropy differential gives

<math display="block">
 \mathrm{d}S = \frac{\mathrm{d}E}{T}-\frac{\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathrm{d}\langle \mathbf J\rangle}{T}
</math>

Comparing this result with the entropy differential given by entropy maximization allows determination of <math>\lambda_0</math> and <math>\boldsymbol\lambda_1</math>

<math display="block"> \lambda_0 = \beta</math>

<math display="block">
 \boldsymbol\lambda_1=-\beta \boldsymbol\omega
</math>

which allows the probability of a given state <math>p_i</math> to be written as

<math display="block"> p_i = \frac{1}{Z}e^{-\beta(E_i-\vec{\omega}\cdot\mathbf J_i)} </math>

which is recognized as the probability of some microstate given a prescribed macrostate using the Gibbs rotational ensemble.<ref name="gibbs"/><ref name="gyro"/><ref name=TD/> The term <math>E_i-\boldsymbol\omega\cdot\mathbf J_i</math> can be recognized as the effective Hamiltonian <math>\mathcal{H}</math> for the system, which then simplifies the Gibbs rotational partition function to that of a normal [[canonical ensemble|canonical]] system

<math display="block"> Z = \sum_i e^{-\beta\mathcal{H}_i} </math>

==Applicability==
The Gibbs rotational ensemble is useful for calculations regarding rotating systems. It is commonly used for describing particle distribution in centrifuges. For example, take a rotating cylinder (height <math>Z</math>, radius <math>R</math>) with fixed particle number <math>N</math>, fixed volume <math>V</math>, fixed average energy <math>\langle E\rangle</math>, and average angular momentum <math>\langle \mathbf J\rangle</math>. The expectation value of [[number density]] of particles <math>\langle n(r)\rangle</math> at radius <math>r</math> can be written as

<math display="block"> \langle n(r)\rangle = \frac{1}{Z} \int n(r) \frac{\mathrm{d}^3 p\; \mathrm{d}^3q}{h^3}e^{-\beta(E-\boldsymbol{\omega}\cdot\mathbf J)} </math>

Using the Gibbs rotational partition function, <math>Z</math> can be calculated to be

<math display="block">
 Z=\frac{\pi ^{5/2} Z \sqrt{\beta m} \left(e^{\frac{1}{2} \beta m R^2 \omega ^2}-1\right)}{\sqrt{2} \beta ^3 h^3 \omega ^2}
</math>

Density of a particle at a given point can be thought of as unity divided by an infinitesimal volume, which can be represented as a delta function.

<math display="block">
 n(r) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{d}r\; r\;\mathrm{d}\theta \;\mathrm{d}z}\rightarrow\frac{\delta(r'-r)\delta(\theta'-\theta)\delta(z'-z)}{r'}
</math>

which finally gives <math>\langle n(r)\rangle</math> as

<math display="block">
 \langle n(r)\rangle=\frac{\beta m \omega ^2}{2\pi Z}\frac{ e^{\frac{1}{2} \beta m r^2 \omega ^2}}{e^{\frac{1}{2} \beta m R^2 \omega ^2}-1}
</math>

which is the expected result.

== Difference between Grand canonical ensemble and Gibbs canonical ensemble ==
The [[Grand canonical ensemble]] and the Gibbs canonical ensemble are two different statistical ensembles used in statistical mechanics to describe systems with different constraints.

The grand canonical ensemble describes a system that can exchange both energy and particles with a reservoir. It is characterized by three variables: the temperature (T), [[chemical potential]] (μ), and volume (V) of the system.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Satoh |first1=A. |title=Introduction to Molecular-Microsimulation of Colloidal Dispersions |chapter=Statistical Ensembles |series=Studies in Interface Science |date=2003 |volume=17 |pages=7–18 |doi=10.1016/S1383-7303(03)80030-3 |isbn=978-0-444-51424-0 |quote=The grand canonical ensemble is a statistical ensemble which is specified by the system volume V, temperature T, and chemical potential μ; the chemical potential is the energy which is necessary for adding one particle to the system adiabatically, and the detailed definition will be shown later. This statistical ensemble is highly appropriate for treating a physical system in which particles and energies can be transported across the walls of the system. }}</ref> The chemical potential determines the average [[particle number]] in this ensemble, which allows for some variation in the number of particles. The grand canonical ensemble is commonly used to study systems with a fixed temperature and chemical potential, but a variable particle number, such as gases in contact with a particle reservoir.<ref>{{Cite web |title=LECTURE 9 Statistical Mechanics |url=https://ps.uci.edu/~cyu/p115A/LectureNotes/Lecture9/html_version/lecture9.html |access-date=2023-05-15 |website=ps.uci.edu}}{{self-published inline|date=August 2025}}</ref>

On the other hand, the Gibbs canonical ensemble describes a system that can exchange energy but has a fixed number of particles. It is characterized by two variables: the temperature (T) and volume (V) of the system. In this ensemble, the energy of the system can fluctuate, but the number of particles remains fixed. The Gibbs canonical ensemble is commonly used to study systems with a fixed temperature and particle number, but variable energy, such as systems in thermal equilibrium.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Emch |first1=Gérard G. |last2=Liu |first2=Chuang |title=The Logic of Thermostatistical Physics |chapter=The Gibbs Canonical Ensembles |date=2002 |pages=331–372 |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-04886-3_10 |isbn=978-3-642-07462-2 }}</ref>
